data.text:
The only thing I want is freedom

And I realized that even money can’t give you that

Recently, I’ve taken a step back from business and gone back to university

Most people said it didn’t make sense, especially since I already had a good money-making method going on…

But there are a couple of reasons why I made that move…

For one, I wanted to migrate out of the Philippines. Although it’s a great country, I experienced its limitations when I traveled to Europe.

It was costly (both in time and money) to get a visa, and there was no certainty of approval when you applied for it.

During this tim, I realized that even if I had an abundance of money, I still wouldn’t have the autonomy to work wherever, whenever, and with whoever I want…

So I decided that I would move to a first-world country (ideally the US or Spain), get citizenship, and acquire a passport that would allow me that freedom.

The problem? The only way I can apply for residency visas in those countries is by:

Having a professional certificate (such as a college degree)
Or by having an established source of income for 5 years

Since I had 1.5 years left in college, I took that route instead.

I figured that I already had experience working a night shift job along with university, so I’ll be able to run the business along with my studies…

But things haven’t been great.

I now see that running a business is completely different from having a night shift job.

A business doesn’t clock in at 9 am and clock out at 5 pm… It’s a full-day activity, constantly demanding your attention and decision-making.

And even though you get results for your clients, you still need to maintain relationships, improve the roadmap, and develop a better client experience

Every single day…

The worst part? Uni isn’t forgiving either…

I have a professor whose building is 30 minutes away from my college building, but she wants you to attend class on time.

If you’re even just a minute late, you won’t be allowed to enter the class.

And if you’re absent 6 times, you automatically fail.

Another professor wants us to memorize the Constitution word for word. One incorrect sentence and you get a 0…

The tough times in business and school has made it hard for me to maintain and grow my relationships and passions (such as content creation).

I’m starting to feel as if I’m losing at everything right now.

Cash flow is down. Grades are struggling. Relationships and creativity are suffering.

Are all of this worth the freedom I seek?

Should I continue to sacrifice what I have in hopes of getting what I want?

Honestly, I don’t know…

I just know that for most of my life, I’ve always been in rock bottom.

An accident child with no father, a fake identity, and no control as to what I should be doing or where I should be…

When things can’t get worse, it seems that anything you do is just… better.

You have nothing to lose. And everything to gain.

This gives you the freedom to look for what you’re willing to die for…

And live for it.

data.text:
A Call for Sobriety Amid Regional Unrest

In recent days, Asia has witnessed a wave of unrest that demands not only attention—but reflection.

🇳🇵 In Nepal, the Gen-Z-led uprising has escalated into one of the most violent political convulsions in recent memory. Sparked by a government-imposed social media ban, the protests have revealed deeper frustrations over corruption, inequality, and generational neglect. As of September 10, at least 22 people have died, including 19 shot by police, and hundreds have been injured 

Prime Minister K.P. Sharma Oli has resigned, but the violence continues. Government buildings—including Parliament, the Supreme Court, and ministers’ homes—have been torched. Former PM Sher Bahadur Deuba and Foreign Minister Arzu Rana were assaulted in the streets 

The army has now been deployed to restore order 

🇮🇩 In Indonesia, protests ignited by revelations of lavish housing allowances for lawmakers—over 10 times the minimum wage—have spread across 32 provinces, including Jakarta and Bali 

The death of Affan Kurniawan, a young delivery driver killed by a police vehicle, has become a symbol of injustice 

Protesters have looted homes of officials, called for the dissolution of parliament, and demanded accountability from President Prabowo Subianto’s administration 

🇵🇭 In the Philippines, we stand at a precipice. The recent exposés on flood control corruption, involving billions in public funds and the flaunting of wealth by contractor families, have shaken public trust 

Senate leadership has shifted amid these revelations, and the names of powerful figures—including House Speaker Romualdez—have emerged in corruption probes 

While protests remain largely online, the anger is real. The question is not whether unrest will come—but whether our leaders will act before it does.

We call for sobriety, not silence. For accountability, not vengeance. For dialogue, not denial.

Let us not wait for fire to reach our doorstep before we listen to the cries of the people. 

President Marcos must act swiftly and decisively—not with rhetoric, but with reform. 

The time for half-measures has passed.

Let us learn from Nepal and Indonesia. Let us not follow.

Let this be a moment of reckoning, not ruin.

Dr. Tony Leachon 

@PhilippineStar 
@iampinglacson

DPWH'S CASINO ROYALE: LACSON LINKS 'BGC BOYS' TO MONEY LAUNDERING

Senate President Pro Tempore Ping Lacson on Tuesday accused five former Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) officials—dubbed the "BGC Boys"—of gambling away taxpayers' money in casinos and possibly laundering funds intended for flood control projects.

In a privilege speech, Lacson said the group—known to casino employees as the Bulacan Group of Contractors—used aliases and fake driver's licenses to conceal their identities while incurring nearly ₱950 million in gross gambling losses across 13 casinos in Metro Manila, Cebu, and Pampanga.

The five were identified as Henry Alcantara, sacked DPWH Region 4A assistant regional director, alias Joseph Castro Villegas; Brice Ericson Hernandez, Bulacan OIC district engineer, alias Marvin Santos de Guzman; Jaypee Mendoza, assistant district engineer, alias Peejay Asuncion; Arjay Domasig, DPWH engineer II, alias Sandro Bernardo Park; and Edrick San Diego.

Lacson cited casino records showing Hernandez lost ₱435 million and Mendoza ₱418 million, while Alcantara, Domasig, and San Diego recorded millions more in losses. Yet the same records also reflected suspicious multimillion-peso winnings, which Lacson said may have been used to legitimize illicit funds.

"Sinuwerte nga kayang sabay sabay na nanalo ang mga ito, Mr. President? O baka naman money laundering scheme?" Lacson said.

He added that their gambling violated Presidential Decree 1869, RA 6713, and other laws prohibiting public officials from entering casinos, while their use of fake IDs and aliases constituted separate criminal offenses.

Because of this, Lacson said he has referred the names and aliases of the five to the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) and sought the freezing of their bank accounts.

"Sumatutal, habang lubog pa rin sa tubig-baha ang mga taga-Bulacan dahil sa mga pangungurakot ng mga ito, at kahit buking na mismo ng Pangulo ang kalokohan, sige pa rin ang pagpapasasa ng BGC Boys — sa pagwawaldas ng pera ng taumbayan. Walang kahiya-hiya sa katawan. Wala pong konsensya ang mga ito, Mr. President," he said.

Beyond accountability, Lacson called for reforms, including a perpetual ban on blacklisted contractors with ghost or substandard projects, heavier penalties for conflicts of interest under the Contractors' License Law and RA 6713, and stricter transparency in the planning and funding of infrastructure projects, including requiring detailed engineering designs before the release of funds.

"Mr. President, these people have reduced the lives of our flood stricken countrymen into living hell. It is time to give them what they rightly deserve," Lacson concluded.
